sections.body: Some puzzles have no singles left. The next technique to try is the NAKED PAIR.

Write the possible numbers (candidates) in small notes in each empty square. A naked pair is two squares in the same row, column or box that both have the same two candidates and nothing else, such as 3 and 8.

Here is why that matters. Those two squares must hold 3 and 8 between them, in one order or the other. So no other square in that row, column or box can be 3 or 8. You can cross 3 and 8 out of all the other squares in that unit.
Example: a row has a pair of squares with notes 3 and 8. Another square in the row has notes 3, 5 and 8. Cross out 3 and 8. Only 5 is left, so that square is 5.
Use the Notes button in the Sudoku game. Look for two squares in a row with exactly the same two notes. Cross those numbers out of the rest of the row.

Naked pairs are the first technique that needs pencil notes. Encourage your child to use the Notes button. If a pair cannot be found, taking a hint from the game is fine: it gives a nudge first, not the answer.

quiz.q: Two squares in a row both have only the notes 3 and 8. Another square in the same row has the notes 3, 5 and 8. What number can it be?
hints: The pair will use up 3 and 8 in this row.
Cross 3 and 8 out of the other square's notes. What is left?
Example: a pair with 2 and 6, and another square with notes 2, 4 and 6, leaves 4. Do the same for this question.
quiz.explain: The pair takes both 3 and 8, so the other square cannot be 3 or 8. Only 5 is left.

quiz.q: Two squares in a box both have only the notes 2 and 6. Another square in the box has the notes 2, 4 and 6. Which number goes in that square?
hints: The pair of squares has to hold 2 and 6 between them.
So the third square cannot be 2 or 6.
Example: a pair with 5 and 9, and a square with notes 1, 5, 7 and 9, leaves 1 and 7. Cross out the pair's numbers here.
quiz.explain: The pair uses up 2 and 6 in the box. The other square can only be 4.

quiz.q: Why can you cross out the pair's numbers from the other squares in that row, column or box?
options: The two pair squares must hold those two numbers between them
Those numbers are too big to be written anywhere else
The rules of the puzzle say that you must always cross out any pair you find
hints: Think about what the two squares must contain.
If the two squares hold 3 and 8 in some order, are any 3s or 8s left for the others?
Example: if two seats can only be taken by Ann and Ben, nobody else can sit there. Use the same idea for numbers.
quiz.explain: Those two squares will use up both numbers, so no other square in the row, column or box can be either one.
